full_story_part1.text: A small slider inside the refrigerator may be easy to ignore. But many crisper drawers have 2 settings: low humidity and high humidity. They are not simply 2 names for the same space. The low setting lets more air move through the drawer. The high setting is more closed. That small difference can matter after fresh food comes home from the store.

full_story_part1.canonical_text:
A small slider inside the refrigerator may be easy to ignore.

But many crisper drawers have two settings: low humidity and high humidity. They are not simply two names for the same space.

The low setting lets more air move through the drawer. The high setting is more closed.

That small difference can matter after fresh food comes home from the store.

full_story_part2.text: Some foods give off a gas as they ripen. Other foods lose water quickly and become soft or limp. The 2 drawer settings are meant for these different problems. There is also one important surprise. The best choice is not always as simple as fruit goes here and vegetables go there. And before choosing a setting, there is another question: does this food belong in the refrigerator at all?

Some foods give off a gas as they ripen. Other foods lose water quickly and become soft or limp. The two drawer settings are meant for these different problems.

There is also one important surprise. The best choice is not always as simple as “fruit goes here” and “vegetables go there.”

And before choosing a setting, there is another question: does this food belong in the refrigerator at all?

point_one.text: A useful way to use the slider is to ask one question: Am I trying to keep water in, or let a gas out? If the main problem is wilting, high humidity is the better match. Leafy greens, such as kale, and broccoli can lose water quickly, so a more closed drawer can help. If the main problem is gas, low humidity may be the better match. Apples and pears give off ethylene, a gas that can make nearby produce ripen too quickly. More air movement helps that gas escape. This turns the slider into a simple diagnosis tool. You do not have to memorize a fruit-and-vegetable rule. You can look at the food's main storage problem.

A useful way to use the slider is to ask one question: “Am I trying to keep water in, or let a gas out?”

If the main problem is wilting, high humidity is the better match. Leafy greens, such as kale, and broccoli can lose water quickly, so a more closed drawer can help.

If the main problem is gas, low humidity may be the better match. Apples and pears give off ethylene, a gas that can make nearby produce ripen too quickly. More air movement helps that gas escape.

This turns the slider into a simple diagnosis tool. You do not have to memorize a fruit-and-vegetable rule. You can look at the food’s main storage problem.

point_two.text: Humidity settings cannot help food that is not suited to refrigerator storage. Tomatoes and bananas are recommended for counter storage, not for a low-humidity drawer. Potatoes, sweet potatoes, onions, and garlic do not need refrigeration and are better kept in a cool, dry place. So even the low-humidity advice for apples and pears should not be copied to every food that gives off ethylene. First choose the right storage place. Then choose the setting.
